language: science
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }

  url: http://127.0.0.1:8239/index.html
  readySelector: "#board svg"

explainClip:
  query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain", id: explain }
  caption: "The particle model"
  say: "Everything is made of tiny particles, with empty space between them."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "Zoom in on ice: particles packed in a pattern, vibrating in place.", say: "Zoom in on ice: particles packed in a pattern, vibrating in place." }
    - wait: 3200

Scientists explain how things behave using a **model**: a simplified picture that's good at explaining and predicting, and the particle model comes down to four ideas.

## Engage: zoom into a drop of water

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a picture of matter first exposes the idea that matter is continuous, or that particles float in something."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Zoom into a drop of water a billion times. What would you see?"
  options: ["Smooth water, all the way down", "Lots of tiny drops of water", "Tiny particles floating in water", "Tiny particles with empty space between them"]
  actual: "Tiny particles with empty space between them, always moving. There is nothing between them, not even air."
```

Decide before you look. There is no penalty for being wrong: the point is to find out what you think now.

## Explore: the zoom lens

```step
stage: run
insight: "Seeing ice, water and steam as the same particles in different arrangements sets up the whole model."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#zoom", height: 500 }
check: { type: board, text: "Look at all three samples: ice, liquid water and steam.", expect: { done: true } }
```

Look at each sample for a few seconds. Watch how the particles are spaced, and how they move.

## Explain: what the model says

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "The four key ideas (particles, space, motion, attraction) are what students must be able to reproduce before they can use diagrams to reason."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "What is between the particles?"
      options: ["Air", "Water", "Nothing: empty space"]
      answer: 2
      feedback: ["Air is made of particles too, so it can't be what fills the gaps between particles.", "The particles are the water, so there is no more water in the gaps between them.", null]
      explain: "There's nothing at all between the particles, not even air."
    hint: ["If you put air in the gaps, what would that air be made of?", "Have a look at the steam sample and at what is drawn in the gaps between the particles."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Do the particles in ice ever stop moving?"
      options: ["Yes, ice is frozen still", "No, they vibrate in place"]
      answer: 1
      feedback: ["Watch the ice sample again and look closely at each particle.", null]
      explain: "Even in a solid the particles vibrate, and they never stop."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Ice, liquid water and steam: are their particles the same?"
      options: ["Yes: only the arrangement and motion change", "No: ice particles are bigger", "No: steam particles are smaller"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Particles never change size, so ice particles can't be bigger than the others.", "Particles never change size, so steam particles can't be smaller either."]
      explain: "All three are made of the same water particles, and only how those particles are arranged and how they move is different."
    hint: ["When you went from ice to steam on the board, was it the particles themselves that looked different, or something about how they sit and move?", "Click between Ice and Steam and keep your eye on a single particle each time."]
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Which statements are part of particle theory?"
      options: ["Part of particle theory", "Not true"]
      items:
        - ["All matter is made of tiny particles.", "Part of particle theory", "This is the first key idea."]
        - ["There is empty space between particles.", "Part of particle theory", "This is the second key idea."]
        - ["Particles are always moving.", "Part of particle theory", "This is the third key idea, and it holds even in solids, where the particles vibrate."]
        - ["Particles attract each other.", "Part of particle theory", "This is the fourth key idea, and the attraction is strongest in solids and weakest in gases."]
        - ["Particles expand when they are heated.", "Not true", "Particles never change size, so when they're heated they move faster and spread out instead."]
        - ["There is air between the particles.", "Not true", "Air is made of particles too, so it can't be in the gaps between particles."]
        - ["Particles in a solid do not move.", "Not true", "Particles in a solid do move, because they vibrate in place."]
      explain: "You can remember the four key ideas as particles, space, motion and attraction."
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each state to its particles: arrangement, motion and attraction."
      pairs:
        - ["Solid", "Close together in a fixed pattern, vibrating in place, strong attraction"]
        - ["Liquid", "Close together with no pattern, sliding past each other, weaker attraction"]
        - ["Gas", "Far apart, moving fast in all directions, very weak attraction"]
      explain: "The three states differ in the same three ways: arrangement, motion and attraction."
    hint: ["Take one state at a time and picture whether its particles stay in a pattern and whether they swap neighbours.", "Flick between Ice and Liquid water on the board and watch whether a particle stays put or moves along to a new neighbour."]
```

### Between the particles

Look at any sample and think about what fills the gaps between the particles.

### Ice

Watch the ice sample for a few seconds and see what each particle is doing.

### Same particles?

Think about what changed between the three samples, and what did not.

### The four key ideas

Sort each statement into the group it belongs to.

### Across the states

Compare the three samples on the board and see how the particles sit and move in each.

## Practise: name that state

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Reliable matching of diagrams to states needs practice with feedback that names the particle feature every time."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#identify", height: 500 }
check: { type: board, text: "Name the state of six substances correctly.", expect: { done: true } }
hint: ["Look first at how close the particles are, and then at whether they stay in place or move around.", "After each answer the line under the board explains it, so if you get one wrong, read it and use it on the next round."]
```

Each round shows a new substance through the zoom lens. Is it a solid, a liquid or a gas?

## Elaborate: explain three things about ice

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Explaining properties in particle language is the move from describing the model to using it."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "For each property of ice, choose the particle explanation."
  options:
    - "Its particles are held in fixed positions by strong attraction"
    - "Its particles are packed closely, with very little space between them"
    - "Its particles vibrate more as they warm, until they break free of their positions"
    - "Its particles are far apart and move freely"
    - "Its particles get bigger when warmed"
  items:
    - ["Ice keeps its shape on a plate.", "Its particles are held in fixed positions by strong attraction", "Strong attraction holds each particle in place."]
    - ["You can't squash an ice cube.", "Its particles are packed closely, with very little space between them", "There is almost no empty space to push the particles into."]
    - ["An ice cube held in your hand starts to melt.", "Its particles vibrate more as they warm, until they break free of their positions", "Warming makes particles vibrate more until they slide past each other."]
  explain: "Each property comes down to one particle feature, which is either arrangement, motion or attraction."
```

On paper: draw a particle diagram of ice and label it with these three explanations.

## Elaborate: build a state

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Spacing and motion go together: building the states from the two features shows why some combinations never happen."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#build", height: 520 }
check: { type: board, text: "Build a solid, a liquid and a gas.", expect: { done: true } }
hint: ["Think about what each state needs from the two choices, how close the particles are and how they move.", "If a combination isn't a real state, the line under the board tells you which state those particles would really make, so use that to change one choice."]
```

Choose how close the particles are and how they move. Try the combinations that don't make a real state too, and read what the board says.

## Elaborate: how good is the model?

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Every model has limits; Brownian motion is the classic evidence that particles exist and move."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Does the particle model explain it?"
      options: ["Explained by the model", "Not explained"]
      items:
        - ["Why a gas spreads to fill its container", "Explained by the model", "Gas particles move fast in all directions."]
        - ["Why you can smell perfume from across a room", "Explained by the model", "Perfume particles move and spread between the air particles."]
        - ["Why copper is orange-brown", "Not explained", "Colour depends on what the particles are made of."]
        - ["Why solids keep their shape", "Explained by the model", "Strong attraction holds particles in place."]
        - ["What particles themselves are made of", "Not explained", "The model treats particles as tiny balls. Atoms come later."]
        - ["Why some substances are poisonous", "Not explained", "That depends on chemistry, not on arrangement or motion."]
      explain: "The model explains how substances behave, not everything about them."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown saw tiny grains from pollen jiggling in water under a microscope, in random directions, with nothing stirring the water. In 1905 Albert Einstein explained it with particles. What causes the jiggling?"
      options: ["The grains are alive and swimming", "Water particles are always moving and keep bumping into the grains", "The water is flowing slowly"]
      answer: 1
      feedback: ["Brown checked this: grains from long-dead plants, and even specks of dust, jiggled the same way.", null, "The jiggling goes in random directions, not along with a flow."]
      explain: "This is Brownian motion, caused by millions of tiny bumps from moving water particles, and it was early strong evidence that particles are real and always moving."
```

### What it explains

### The evidence

## Elaborate: designing with materials

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Designers in Design and Technologies choose solids, liquids and gases for exactly these particle reasons."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Match each design choice to the particle reason."
  options:
    - "A gas can be squashed, so it cushions bumps"
    - "A liquid hardly squashes, so a push at one end moves the other end straight away"
    - "Solid particles are held in fixed positions, so the shape stays under a load"
    - "Its particles are lighter"
  items:
    - ["Bike tyres are filled with air, not water.", "A gas can be squashed, so it cushions bumps", "Air particles have space to move closer when you hit a bump."]
    - ["Car brakes use a liquid in the pipes to push the brake pads.", "A liquid hardly squashes, so a push at one end moves the other end straight away", "A gas would just squash instead of passing the push along."]
    - ["Bridge beams are made of solid steel.", "Solid particles are held in fixed positions, so the shape stays under a load", "Strong attraction keeps the steel particles in place."]
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my first prediction with the particle model and can say what changed in my thinking." }
```

Go back to your prediction in Engage. Was matter smooth, drops, particles in water, or particles with empty space? Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- All matter is made of tiny particles; there is empty space between them; they are always moving; they attract each other.
- **Solid:** close together in a fixed pattern, vibrating in place.
- **Liquid:** close together with no pattern, sliding past each other.
- **Gas:** far apart, moving fast in all directions.
- There is nothing between particles: not air, not water.

```teacher
summary: Students build the particle model's four key ideas (particles, space,
  motion, attraction) and match particle diagrams to solids, liquids and gases
  (AC9S7U05, node 1, a hinge node).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 7 min · Explain 6 min · Practise 5 min · Evaluate 3
  min · Typical and Wider add about 10 min
goals:
  - I can state the four key ideas of particle theory.
  - I can match a particle diagram to a solid, a liquid or a gas.
  - I can describe how arrangement and motion differ between the three states.
before: >
  This is a concept tutorial for introducing the model or revising it, not a
  replacement for the practical. Run it before hands-on work with states
  (melting ice, a sealed syringe of air). Set the width in the link you share:
  `?width=minimum`, `?width=typical` (the default) or `?width=wider`. Students
  can widen but not narrow.


  The node's response mode is consolidation, so the Practise step (six correct
  identifications, with feedback naming the particle feature each time) is part
  of the minimum path.
running:
  - "Engage: students lock in a prediction before the zoom lens opens. Ask who
    chose 'particles floating in water' and why; it is the most common answer."
  - "Explore: insist they watch the ice for a few seconds. 'Frozen still' is the
    misconception the second Explain question targets."
  - "Explain: the four key ideas are the hinge. Have students say them aloud in
    order: particles, space, motion, attraction."
  - "Practise: six correct, not six in a row. Listen for students naming a
    feature, not just a state."
  - "Evaluate: the 'At first I thought… Now I think…' sentence is worth
    collecting as an exit card."
struggle: Accepting empty space between particles, with nothing in it. When a
  student puts air between the particles, ask what air is made of.
stuck:
  - see: A student says there is air between the particles.
    ask: What is air made of?
    fix: "Air is particles too. Between any particles there is nothing at all: empty
      space."
  - see: A student labels a liquid diagram as a solid because the particles touch.
    ask: Is there a pattern? Do the particles stay in place?
    fix: Solids and liquids are both close together. The difference is the fixed
      pattern and the motion.
  - see: A student says particles get bigger when heated.
    ask: In the zoom lens, did any particle change size between ice and steam?
    fix: Particles never change size; the spaces between them do.
stretch: Why can't particles that are far apart stay still? Use the Build a
  state board to argue it.
support: Give students the four key ideas on a card for the Practise step, and
  ask them to point to the feature they used each time.
leads: >
  Next: node 2 uses the diagrams to reason (why gases fill containers, why
  solids keep their shape). Node 3 explains properties such as compressibility
  and density.


  In class: follow with real samples (an ice cube, water, a sealed syringe of
  air) and ask students to draw the particle view of each.
exit:
  q: Name the four key ideas of particle theory.
  a: All matter is made of particles; there is empty space between them; they are
    always moving; they attract each other.
explain: >
  Everything is made of **particles** far too small to see.


  1. All matter is made of particles.

  2. There is **empty space** between them: nothing at all, not even air.

  3. They are always **moving**. In a solid they vibrate in place.

  4. They **attract** each other: strongly in a solid, weakly in a gas.


  Solids, liquids and gases are the same kind of particles arranged and moving
  differently.
```
